messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 24.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Design an interface circuit for a piezoelectric energy harvester.
    *   Inputs: Piezo (current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$, capacitance $C_p$, leakage 20 MΩ).
    *   Output: Power a load $R_L$ from a storage capacitor at node `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Operating Conditions:
        *   S1: Nominal ($I_p=50\text{uA}, f=100\text{Hz}, R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$)
        *   S2: Heavy load ($R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$) $\rightarrow$ risk of $v_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$
        *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($I_p=100\text{uA}, R_L=2200\text{k}\Omega$) $\rightarrow$ risk of $v_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$
        *   S4: Weak excitation ($I_p=30\text{uA}, R_L=1000\text{k}\Omega$) $\rightarrow$ risk of $v_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$
        *   S5: Low frequency ($f=80\text{Hz}, R_L=470\text{k}\Omega$)
        *   S6: $C_p + 20\%$, Hot ($C_p=30\text{nF}, R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$)

    *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) failed on S2 (low voltage), S3 (overvoltage, ripple), S4 (low voltage), and S5 (settling time).
    *   The piezo voltage is low ($\approx 3.2\text{V}$ open circuit). FBR loses about $0.5\text{V}$ (two Schottky diodes).
    *   The open-circuit voltage is $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p}$. For S1: $V_{oc} = \frac{50\text{uA}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
    *   With FBR, the peak voltage at the output is roughly $V_{oc} - 2 \cdot V_d \approx 3.18 - 0.5 = 2.68\text{V}$.
    *   The average voltage $v_{avg}$ will be lower depending on the load $R_L$.

    *   The FBR is passive. To improve efficiency and boost voltage, we can use:
        1.  **Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE)** or **Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)**.
        2.  **Zener clamping** to prevent $v_{max}$ from exceeding 3.6V (especially for S3).
        3.  **A large storage capacitor** to reduce ripple $v_{pp}$.
    *   SSHI (non-inverting or inverting) uses an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage across $C_p$, effectively increasing the voltage extracted per cycle.
    *   A basic SSHI-like circuit:
        *   Rectifier to charge $C_{out}$.
        *   Switch + Inductor to invert the piezo voltage at peaks.

    *   The most common and effective "simple" active harvester is the SSHI (or a simplified version like Parallel-SSHI).
    *   Wait, looking at the constraints, we need $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ even for S2 ($R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$, $P \approx 1.8^2 / 150\text{k} = 21.6\text{uW}$) and S4 ($I_p=30\text{uA}, R_L=1\text{M}\Omega, P \approx 3.24\text{uW}$).
    *   To handle S3's overvoltage, a Zener diode (DZ33) is essential.

    *   *Simple Synchronous Rectification* (instead of FBR) could reduce the drop.
    *   *SSHI (Parallel)*:
        *   Rectifier (D1, D2) to $C_{out}$.
        *   L1 and Switch S1 in parallel with $C_p$ (between `pzp` and `pzn`).
        *   The switch closes at the peaks of the piezo voltage to flip the charge.

    *   Let's try a **Parallel-SSHI** inspired approach:
        - Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        - Half-bridge rectifier: D1 (`pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`), D2 (`pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`). (Wait, this requires `pzn` to be connected to something else. Usually, we use a full bridge or a center-tapped source).
        - Since the piezo is a source between `pzp` and `pzn`, a full bridge is safer, but we can use a SYNC switch to replace diodes for higher efficiency. However, we only have 4 switches.
        - Let's use a full bridge of Schottky diodes (DSCH) for simplicity and add an SSHI inversion loop.
        - SSHI Loop: L1 between `pzp` and a node `n1`, Switch S1 between `n1` and `pzn`. Controlled by SYNC G1.
        - This flips the voltage across the piezo at the peaks.
        - Storage Capacitor $C_{out}$ at node `out`.
        - Zener DZ33 between `out` and `0` to clamp $v_{max}$ at 3.3-3.6V.

    *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    *   Full Bridge:
        - D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        - D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        - D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (Wait, the prompt says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]").
    *   Inversion:
        - L1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
        - S1: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
        - G1 (SYNC): `edges: both`, `ton: pi*sqrt(L*Cp)`. (Tuning will handle $L$ and $ton$).
    *   Output:
        - C1: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0`
        - DZ1: `0` $\rightarrow$ `out` (zener clamp)

    *   S2 (Heavy load): SSHI significantly increases the extracted energy compared to FBR.
    *   S3 (Strong excitation): DZ33 prevents $v_{out}$ from exceeding 3.6V.
    *   S4 (Weak excitation): Higher efficiency of SSHI helps maintain $v_{out} \ge 1.8\text{V}$.
    *   Ripple: Large $C_{out}$ will minimize $v_{pp}$.

    - D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
    - D2: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
    - D3: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
    - D4: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
    - L1: `pzp`, `n1`
    - S1: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0, ton: ... )
    - C1: `out`, `0`
    - DZ1: `0`, `out` (DZ33)

    *Wait*, let's check if this is too many components.
    D1-D4 (4), L1 (1), S1 (1), G1 (1), C1 (1), DZ1 (1) = 9 components. Well within the 16 limit.

    *Wait*, let's refine the SSHI part. In standard Parallel-SSHI, the inductor is in parallel with the piezo and is switched at the peaks.
    The current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ and $C_p$ are in parallel.
    The voltage $v_{pzp} - v_{pzn}$ is what we want to flip.
    So the inductor $L$ and switch $S$ should be in parallel with the piezo.
    Nodes: `pzp` and `pzn`.
    $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S$ from `n1` to `pzn`. This is a series L-S combination in parallel with the piezo. Correct.

    Is a full bridge necessary?
    A full bridge takes the absolute value of the piezo voltage.
    $V_{out} = |V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}| - 2V_d$.
    If we use a half-bridge, we need a center tap or a DC offset. The piezo is a current source between two nodes, so a full bridge is the most direct way.

    *One more check on the Zener*: The goal is $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. DZ33 breaks down at 3.3V. This should keep $v_{max}$ around 3.3-3.4V, which is $< 3.6\text{V}$.

    *S4 Weak excitation check*: $I_p = 30\text{uA}, R_L = 1\text{M}\Omega, v_{avg}=1.8\text{V} \implies P_{load} = 3.24\text{uW}$.
    The open circuit power is $P_{oc} = \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 \cdot 2f = C_p (\frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p})^2 \cdot 2f = \frac{I_p^2}{2\pi^2 f C_p}$.
    For S4: $P_{oc} = \frac{(30\text{e-6})^2}{2\pi^2 \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}} \approx 5.7\text{uW}$.
    FBR might not be enough, but SSHI (which can theoretically extract more than $P_{oc}$ if the internal resistance is low, though realistically it just approaches it better) should help.

    *L and ton values*:
    $L$ is usually in the mH range. Let's try $L = 10\text{mH}$.
    $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{e-3} \cdot 25\text{e-9}} \approx \pi \sqrt{2.5\text{e-10}} \approx \pi \cdot 1.58\text{e-5} \approx 50\text{uS}$.
    The automatic optimizer will refine these.

    -- `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
    -- `pzn` to `out` (DSCH)
    -- `0` to `pzp` (DSCH)
    -- `0` to `pzn` (DSCH)
    -- `pzp` to `n1` (L)
    -- `n1` to `pzn` (S)
    -- `out` to `0` (C)
    -- `0` to `out` (DZ33)
    -- SYNC G1 controls S1.

    Wait, look at the FBR failure for S3: `vmax = 5.72 V` (FAIL), `vpp = 84.4 mV` (FAIL).
    The ripple $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ is quite tight. This means we need a larger $C_{out}$ and potentially a better way to smooth the voltage.
    Also, the `settled` check `dv <= 0.02 V` might fail if the capacitor is too small and the output oscillates.

    Let's double check the bridge diodes:
    `["pzp", "out"]` - D1
    `["pzn", "out"]` - D2
    `["0", "pzp"]` - D3
    `["0", "pzn"]` - D4
    This is the standard full bridge given in the prompt.

    Wait, is there a better way to handle the ripple?
    A larger $C_{out}$ (e.g., $22\text{uF}$ instead of $2.2\text{uF}$) would reduce $v_{pp}$.
    The prompt allows capacitors up to $47\text{uF}$.

    Let's re-verify the L-S in parallel with $C_p$:
    The piezo is $I_p \sin(\omega t) || C_p || R_{leak}$.
    Connecting an $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with this will create a resonant circuit when $S$ is closed.
    The current $I_C = C_p \frac{dv}{dt}$ will flow into the inductor.
    When $S$ is closed at the peak of $v_{pzp}-v_{pzn}$, the charge on $C_p$ is transferred to $L$ and then flipped back to $C_p$ as $L$ discharges.
    This flips the voltage across $C_p$ from $+V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$ (ideally).
    This effectively doubles the voltage available to the rectifier in each half-cycle.

    One detail: `phase`.
    The peak of $v_{pzp}-v_{pzn}$ occurs at the zero crossing of $I_p \sin(\omega t)$?
    No, $v_{pzp} - v_{pzn} = \int \frac{I_p \sin(\omega t)}{C_p} dt = -\frac{I_p}{\omega C_p} \cos(\omega t)$.
    The voltage peaks when $\cos(\omega t) = \pm 1$, which is when $\omega t = 0, \pi, 2\pi...$
    The current $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ is zero at $\omega t = 0, \pi, 2\pi...$
    So the voltage peaks *do* occur at the zero crossings of the current.
    The SYNC controller closes its switches at the "piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
    So `phase: 0.0` and `edges: "both"` should be correct for SSHI.

    Let's finalize the component list.
    C1 (storage): $10\text{uF}$
    L1: $10\text{mH}$
    S1: controlled by G1
    G1: `ton=50uS`, `edges="both"`, `phase=0.0`
    D1-D4: DSCH
    DZ1: DZ33
    RL: (added by test bench)

    Wait, one last check on the Zener:
    S3 has $I_p = 100\text{uA}, R_L = 2200\text{k}\Omega$.
    Without a clamp, $V_{out}$ would rise until $P_{in} = P_{load}$.
    $P_{in} \approx \frac{I_p^2}{2\pi^2 f C_p} = \frac{(100\text{e-6})^2}{2\pi^2 \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}} \approx 20\text{uW}$.
    $P_{load} = \frac{V_{out}^2}{2.2\text{M}\Omega} \implies V_{out} = \sqrt{20\text{e-6} \cdot 2.2\text{e6}} = \sqrt{44} \approx 6.6\text{V}$.
    This exceeds $3.6\text{V}$, so the Zener is necessary.

    Let's consider the `startup` time $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    A very large $C_{out}$ might slow down the startup.
    $10\text{uF}$ at $1.8\text{V}$ requires $Q = 18\text{uC}$.
    Energy per cycle in S1: $E \approx \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{peak}^2 \times 2 = 25\text{nF} \cdot (3.2\text{V})^2 \approx 256\text{nJ}$.
    Per second (100 Hz): $25.6\text{uJ}$.
    Power: $25.6\text{uW}$.
    To reach $1.8\text{V}$ with $10\text{uF}$ from $0\text{V}$: $E_{stored} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10\text{uF} \cdot 1.8^2 \approx 16.2\text{uJ}$.
    This should be very fast ($< 1\text{s}$), so $10\text{uF}$ is fine. Actually, $10\text{uF}$ is quite small compared to the energy harvested over 0.4s.

    Final Component Count:
    1. D1: DSCH [pzp, out]
    2. D2: DSCH [pzn, out]
    3. D3: DSCH [0, pzp]
    4. D4: DSCH [0, pzn]
    5. L1: 10mH [pzp, n1]
    6. S1: [n1, pzn] (G1)
    7. G1: SYNC [ton=50uS, edges=both, phase=0]
    8. C1: 10uF [out, 0]
    9. DZ1: DZ33 [0, out]
    Total: 9 components.

    Check: `S1: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    These match the requested "full bridge" orientation.

    Wait, I'll use a slightly smaller $C_{out}$ like $4.7\text{uF}$ just to be safer with $t_{up}$, and the optimizer can increase it if $v_{pp}$ is too high. $2.2\text{uF}$ was used in FBR and had $v_{pp} = 26\text{mV}$ for S1, which is ok. But S3 had $84\text{mV}$, which is FAIL. S3 has a much higher $R_L$, so the ripple is actually dominated by the piezo's switching rather than the load. No, that's not right. In S3, the energy harvested per cycle is higher, and the load is lighter, so the voltage rises more. The ripple is $\Delta V = \frac{I_{peak} \cdot t_{on}}{C_{out}}$. With SSHI, $I_{peak}$ is higher, so we might need a larger $C_{out}$. Let's stick with $10\text{uF}$ or $22\text{uF}$.

    Let's use $C1 = 22\text{uF}$.
